strengths: The paper proposes a useful, well-motivated combination of density-ratio Bayesian optimization and graph-based semi-supervised learning. Supporting both sampled unlabeled points and predefined candidate pools gives the approach practical scope. The contribution can be meaningful despite relying on established classifiers.

The empirical results are promising, particularly on the synthetic functions and NATS-Bench. Comparisons include BORE and LFBO with several classifier families, alongside GP-based methods. Twenty repetitions and reported standard errors provide useful evidence of performance beyond illustrative trajectories.

The appendices contain substantial sensitivity analyses covering bandwidth, unlabeled sample count, sampling distribution, pool subsampling, and threshold ratio. The paper also acknowledges computational limitations and the mismatch between existing semi-supervised learning theory and sequential optimization.
weaknesses: The central benefit of unlabeled data is not isolated convincingly. In Figure 12, the no-transduction estimator is competitive and sometimes substantially better, including on Bukin6 and Branin with label spreading. This ablation fixes beta at 0.5, whereas the main comparisons optimize beta. A matched Nadaraya-Watson baseline with adaptive bandwidth and identical acquisition optimization is needed across the main benchmarks. The randomized treatment of acquisition plateaus also needs an ablation. These controls matter because kernel modeling, bandwidth adaptation, and randomization could explain gains attributed to semi-supervision.

The explanation for improved exploration exceeds the supporting analysis. Sampling truncated Gaussians around observed points does not ensure Assumption 4.1: high-density connections can cross the objective's threshold-defined class boundary. Appendix D does not establish that the proposed procedure reduces the defined margin or that expanding a positive-class region improves exploration under argmax selection. Its cited learning bounds are explicitly inapplicable to the adaptive setting. Quantitative exploration diagnostics or a more carefully qualified empirical interpretation would strengthen the central argument.

Acquisition optimization is insufficiently specified to assess comparison fairness. Section 5 specifies L-BFGS-B with 1,000 initializations, but several tasks have finite candidate pools, especially the irregular MNIST embedding pool. The procedure for selecting a valid pool member is unclear, as is acquisition optimization for piecewise-constant tree classifiers and whether competing methods receive the same plateau-handling heuristic. These choices can materially affect optimization performance. A random-search baseline would also help establish benchmark difficulty.

The evidence for applicability beyond low-dimensional problems is limited. All continuous synthetic functions are two-dimensional. The 64-dimensional MNIST experiment uses an embedding trained on 440,000 labeled examples to predict the same three-digit target subsequently optimized. Although the data splits are separate, this supplies substantial target-specific structure. The result therefore supports optimization in a strongly supervised representation; an additional benchmark without this auxiliary target supervision would strengthen broader applicability.

Important reproduction details remain unspecified, including input scaling, the label-spreading clamping factor, propagation stopping settings, and bandwidth optimization bounds and initialization. These are consequential for a distance-based method whose bandwidth sensitivity is demonstrated experimentally. A smaller mathematical presentation issue is the inconsistent transition convention: the entrywise definition of p_ij is column-normalized, while P = D^-1 W is row-normalized and Equation 11 applies P transposed. The intended implementation should be clarified.
